result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.traveling_salesman()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a short route that visits every node (traveling salesperson problem). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L54310-L54463){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.traveling_salesman( nodes=None, cycle=True, method=None, weighted=None, seed=None, max_iterations=10, n_inner=100, move="1-1", temperature=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Traveling salesman](/assets/graphs/traveling-salesman.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Five sites A to E on a pentagon, joined by roads weighted with travel times: A–B 2, B–C 2, C–D 3, D–E 2, E–A 3, and the two chords A–C 4 and B–E 3. The round trip starts at A (outlined) and follows the accent arrows A, B, C, D, E, back to A, visiting every site once; the chords are faded. The card shows the route and its cost 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12." width="100%"} The traveling salesperson problem asks for the cheapest round trip that visits each of a set of locations exactly once. Here the graph does not need to be complete: the route moves between consecutive stops along shortest paths, so the problem is solved on the *metric closure* (see `metric_closure()`) and the returned walk may pass through other nodes on the way. The problem is NP-hard, so the methods are heuristics that give good, but not always optimal, routes. Typical uses are delivery and service routes, drilling and printing orders, and sequencing samples or jobs. Methods: - `"christofides"` (default for undirected graphs): at most 1.5 times the optimal cost. - `"greedy"`: nearest neighbor from the first node; fast, no guarantee. - `"simulated_annealing"` and `"threshold_accepting"`: start from the greedy route and improve it with random moves (`"threshold_accepting"` is the default for directed graphs, where Christofides does not apply). Use `seed=` for reproducible results. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : The stops to visit (IDs or labels). If `None` (default), every node. [cycle]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), return to the start. If `False`, return a path instead: the most expensive leg of the round trip is removed. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : One of the methods above. If `None` (default), `"christofides"` for undirected and `"threshold_accepting"` for directed graphs. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights as travel costs. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag; with `False` every edge costs `1`. Weights must be non-negative. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for the local search methods. [max_iterations]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: stop after this many outer rounds without an improvement. [n_inner]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: moves tried per outer round. [move]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["1-1"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: `"1-1"` (default) swaps two stops, `"1-0"` moves one stop to a new position. [temperature]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Local search only: the starting temperature for simulated annealing (default `100`) or the starting threshold for threshold accepting (default `1`). These are in units of edge weight, so scale them with your weights. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The walk as node IDs. With `cycle=True`, the first and last node are the same. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a stop cannot be reached from another, a weight is negative, `method="christofides"` is used on a directed graph, or an argument is invalid. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Distances between stops are computed with Dijkstra's algorithm from every stop. On that complete, metric instance, Christofides' algorithm (1976) builds a minimum spanning tree, adds a minimum-weight perfect matching on its odd-degree nodes (Edmonds' blossom algorithm), walks an Eulerian circuit of the union, and skips repeated nodes; the triangle inequality makes the result at most $\tfrac{3}{2}$ times optimal, in $O(k^3)$ time for $k$ stops. Simulated annealing accepts a worse route with probability $e^{-\Delta / T}$ and cools $T$ by 1% per round; threshold accepting accepts any move worse by at most the threshold, which shrinks by 10% per round with an accepted move. Both follow NetworkX's design, but unlike NetworkX they leave the current route unchanged when a move is rejected. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Five sites linked by roads, weighted by travel time. The route visits every site and returns to the start, for a total of 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12: ::: {#71122759 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) g.add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 2.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "D", 3.0), ("D", "E", 2.0), ("E", "A", 3.0), ("A", "C", 4.0), ("B", "E", 3.0), ] ) route = g.traveling_salesman() [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in route] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'A'] ``` ::: ::: Only some nodes may need a visit. With stops A and D, the round trip passes through B and C (which are not stops) in both directions, because the path is the only way between them: ::: {#0ef301f7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) path.add_edges([("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 1.0), ("C", "D", 1.0)]) [path.get_label_from_id(n) for n in path.traveling_salesman(nodes=["A", "D"])] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'C', 'B', 'A'] ``` ::: ::: With `cycle=False` the most expensive leg of the round trip (E-A or C-D, weight 3) is dropped, leaving a one-way route: ::: {#d969365b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in g.traveling_salesman(cycle=False, method="greedy")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['D', 'E', 'A', 'B', 'C'] ``` ::: :::
